# RepoCortex — Complete Technical Documentation
> Consolidated reference manual for LLMs, AI coding assistants, and automated indexing engines.

---


# --- BEGIN FILE: llms.txt ---

# RepoCortex

> Deterministic Code Intelligence & Change Safety Engine for AI Coding Agents. 100% local, zero-CGO, compiler-backed relational code graph served over Model Context Protocol (MCP) to Cursor, Claude Code, Windsurf, Google Antigravity, and Zed.

RepoCortex solves the agent token-waste and hallucination problem. Instead of forcing AI agents to run 15+ exploratory greps across hundreds of thousands of lines of code—burning 35,000+ tokens and missing dynamic dispatch or interface implementations—RepoCortex indexes the repository locally into a relational SQLite knowledge graph with four calibrated provenance tiers (`exact`, `high`, `medium`, `low`). Agents query exact call hierarchies, blast radii, database access patterns, and covering tests in single sub-millisecond MCP calls.

## Key Facts & Technical Specifications
- **CLI Commands**: `cortex` (primary), with `repocortex` and `cortex` aliases
- **Runtime Dependencies**: Zero external dependencies, pure Go 1.25+, zero CGO, embedded SQLite (`modernc.org/sqlite`)
- **Supported Languages**: Go, TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, Java, C#, Rust, C/C++, Ruby, PHP, Kotlin, Swift, Scala
- **Protocol**: Model Context Protocol (MCP) over stdio JSON-RPC
- **Storage**: Local `.cortex/index.db` (backwards-compatible with `.cortex/index.db`)
- **Memory Footprint**: < 250 MB RAM for 10,000 source files; sub-50ms incremental watch latency

## MCP Tools Reference
- `get_task_context(task, max_tokens)`: Resolves entry-point files, symbols, upstream callers, downstream callees, and covering tests for a task description in a single call.
- `impact_analysis(symbol, depth)`: Computes the transitive blast radius of modifying a symbol with hub-pruning for loggers and base utilities.
- `find_tests(symbol)`: Identifies covering test functions discovered along proven call paths rather than filename guessing.
- `find_callers(symbol)`: Traces direct upstream callers entering a symbol.
- `find_symbol(name)`: Looks up exact symbol definitions and their type signatures.
- `find_references(symbol)`: Finds all cross-file references with calibrated confidence.
- `search_code(query)`: High-performance SQLite FTS5 BM25 search across indexed code symbols and docstrings.
- `get_project_overview()`: Summarizes repository language breakdown, symbol counts, and index health.
- `detect_blindspots(file)`: Reports unresolved references, orphan tables, and unmapped endpoints.
- `plan_change(task, targets)`: Generates an ordered refactoring sequence with test verification gates.

## Core CLI Commands
- `cortex init`: Initialize the local `.cortex/` SQLite database schema.
- `cortex index`: Extract AST definitions, imports, and references across all supported files.
- `cortex resolve`: Bind extracted references to definitions and construct the directional call graph.
- `cortex install --rules`: Auto-detect installed agents (Cursor, Claude Code, Windsurf, Antigravity) and inject MCP config and behavioral rules.
- `cortex impact --base <rev> --head <rev>`: Calculate the exact blast radius between two Git revisions.
- `cortex missed --fail-on high`: Audit code blindspots, unmapped HTTP routes, and uncalled symbols.
- `cortex arch --fail-on high`: Enforce declarative architectural boundary invariants.
- `cortex report pr --impact impact.json`: Generate bounded, formatted GitHub Pull Request review comments.
- `cortex report sarif`: Output standard SARIF 2.1.0 for GitHub Code Scanning integration.
- `cortex ui`: Launch the embedded offline visual architecture portal at `http://localhost:7777`.

## Documentation Links
- [60-Second Quickstart](docs/USER_GUIDE.md): Step-by-step setup, index creation, and agent wiring
- [Why Not Vector RAG?](docs/WHY_NOT_VECTOR_RAG.md): Technical deep-dive on why deterministic graphs outperform vector similarity search for source code
- [Complete CLI Manual](docs/CLI.md): Comprehensive reference of all 35+ CLI subcommands and options
- [Architecture & Design](docs/DESIGN_AND_ARCHITECTURE.md): System architecture, in-memory CSR graph, and design invariants
- [Agent Integration Guide](docs/agent-integration.md): Setup instructions for Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Desktop, Antigravity
- [Accuracy & Benchmarks](docs/accuracy.md): Precision and recall measurements against compiler ground truth across 30,000+ edges
- [Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)](docs/FAQ.md): Answers to common questions regarding performance, scalability, and security

# --- BEGIN FILE: docs/WHY_NOT_VECTOR_RAG.md ---

# Why Vector RAG Fails for Code: The Case for Deterministic Graph Intelligence

*An engineering perspective on why vector embeddings and semantic search break down on real codebases, and why deterministic AST graphs with calibrated confidence tiers are the only reliable foundation for AI coding agents.*

---

## 1. The Siren Song of Vector Similarity

Every engineer who has plugged an LLM into a codebase starts with the same architecture:
1. Chunk source files into 500-token windows.
2. Run them through an embedding model (`text-embedding-3-small`, Ada, etc.).
3. Store the vectors in a vector database.
4. When a user or agent asks a question, retrieve the top-10 nearest chunks by cosine similarity and dump them into the prompt.

On paper, this sounds elegant. It requires almost zero language-specific parsing, works on any programming language from day one, and handles natural language questions gracefully.

In practice—on real production repositories with 500,000 lines of code, overloaded methods, microservice boundaries, and subtle interface contracts—**it fails continuously, silently, and expensively.**

Why? Because natural language and computer software operate on completely different mathematical foundations:
- **Prose is continuous and fuzzy.** If a user manual mentions *"resetting your credentials"* and another paragraph mentions *"updating your password"*, they are semantically similar. Cosine similarity correctly bridges that vocabulary gap.
- **Code is discrete and causal.** If a function is named `processPayment()`, it does not matter how semantically similar it is to `verifyPayment()`, `logPayment()`, or `mockPayment()`. If the runtime executes `BillingGateway.settle()`, then **only** `settle()` matters. 

Embedding similarity measures **lexical and thematic proximity**. Compilers, linkers, and runtimes operate on **causal reachability**. Conflating the two is the root cause of AI coding agent hallucinations.

---

## 2. The Five Fatal Traps of Code RAG

Through months of testing agents across large polyglot enterprise codebases, we documented five failure modes that vector RAG cannot fix without fundamentally abandoning vector search:

### Trap 1: The "Unrelated Payment Marketing" Paradox (Similarity $\neq$ Causality)

Consider a real scenario from our benchmark fixtures:
A user asks an AI agent:
> *"Add idempotency token verification to our payment callback processing."*

A vector RAG system embeds this prompt and queries the vector index.
- In `internal/billing/CallbackController.java`, the code defines `handleWebhook(Request req)`: concise, dense, few comments.
- In `unrelated/marketing/MarketingReport.java`, a developer wrote a lengthy class comment explaining:
  > *"This report aggregates marketing attribution. Unrelated to payment processing callbacks, which are handled in billing."*

The vector search engine computes the dot product. Because `MarketingReport.java` repeats the words *"payment"*, *"processing"*, and *"callbacks"* multiple times in natural prose, **it scores higher in cosine similarity than the actual controller code!**

The vector database happily feeds `MarketingReport.java` into the agent's context window. The agent dutifully reads it, gets confused, greps for more files, burns tokens, and misses the actual callback handler.

> **Engineering Principle**: Graph connectivity (can symbol A reach symbol B through an actual AST call edge?) must act as an **admission gate**, not merely a ranking heuristic.

---

### Trap 2: The Blast Radius Blindspot

When an engineer or an agent modifies a function signature—say, renaming `UpdateUser(ctx, id)` or adding a mandatory parameter—the most dangerous question is:
> *"Who across the entire repository breaks if I make this change?"*

Vector search cannot answer this question. Period.
- If function `A()` calls `B()`, they may share zero vocabulary. `A()` might be a generic task scheduler `RunBatchJob()`, and `B()` might be `RotateKey()`. No embedding model on earth will score them as close neighbors.
- What an agent actually needs is a **reverse transitive reachability walk** along proven call edges.
- If an agent relies on vector search or grep to find callers, it misses callers whose function names or surrounding comments don't resemble the target. The agent submits a PR, tests pass locally because tests only ran on modified files, and staging breaks with a runtime panic.

---

### Trap 3: Symbol Collision and the "Close()" Illusion

In any production codebase with more than 50 packages, common identifier names collide constantly:
- `Close()` appears on database connections, HTTP response bodies, file handles, channel wrappers, and metrics flushers.
- `Init()` or `Start()` appears in dozens of subsystems.
- `Process()` or `Execute()` exists on command handlers, workers, pipelines, and CLI commands.

To a vector model, all instances of `db.Close()` and `file.Close()` live in the same neighborhood of vector space. 
When an agent asks *"find references to Close"*, vector retrieval retrieves a noisy salad of unrelated clean-up methods.

To resolve a reference correctly, you need:
1. **Lexical scoping** (what package is imported?)
2. **Type attribution** (what is the receiver type of `db`?)
3. **AST arity checking** (how many arguments does the call pass?)
4. **Interface satisfaction** (does this struct implement that interface?)

None of these four operations are vectors. They are discrete relational algebra queries over an Abstract Syntax Tree.

---

### Trap 4: Context Window Pollution and the "Lost in the Middle" Tax

A typical vector RAG pipeline retrieves the top 10–20 chunks (often 500–1,000 tokens each) to maximize recall. That dumps **10,000 to 20,000 tokens of raw file text** into the agent's prompt on every turn.

This introduces two severe penalties:
1. **Financial and Latency Tax**: At current frontier model pricing, 20k tokens per prompt across a 30-turn agent coding session burns \$1.50–\$5.00 per task and adds 5–15 seconds of time-to-first-token per request.
2. **Cognitive Degradation ("Lost in the Middle")**: Extensive academic research demonstrates that LLM reasoning degrades sharply when critical needles are surrounded by large haystacks of irrelevant code. When the context is polluted with 80% irrelevant snippets, the agent produces weaker reasoning and introduces subtle logic bugs.

RepoCortex flips this equation. Instead of returning whole files or raw text chunks:
- It returns **compact symbol signatures and 2-hop subgraphs**.
- A full task context (the target file, exact callers, related database tables, and the specific test file) typically costs **under 800 tokens**.
- The agent gets 95% less noise and 100% higher causal precision.

---

### Trap 5: The Zero-Provenance Lie

When a vector search engine returns a list of results, each result carries a float score:
`[Score: 0.8421, File: payment.go]`

What does `0.8421` mean to an autonomous agent?
- Does it mean the compiler proved that `payment.go` executes this code?
- Does it mean an import statement matches?
- Does it mean someone mentioned "payment" in a TODO comment three years ago?

The agent cannot tell. Because every result is presented with equal epistemic weight, the agent treats heuristic hunches as absolute facts. It deletes code thinking nobody calls it, or writes callers that fail at link time.

---

## 3. The RepoCortex Alternative: Deterministic Graph Intelligence

We built RepoCortex because we were tired of watching agents flounder in vector soup. We wanted a tool built on the same principles as compilers, linkers, and databases: **deterministic truth, provable provenance, and bounded memory.**

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        THE REPOCORTEX GRAPH PIPELINE                      |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                                                         |
|   Source Code (.go, .ts, .py, .java, .rs, .c, etc.)                     |
|        │                                                                |
|        ▼ (Tree-Sitter / SCIP Indexers)                                  |
|   AST Extraction (Pure Go, 206 grammars, zero CGO)                      |
|        │                                                                |
|        ▼                                                                |
|   Symbol & Reference Registry (SQLite relational tables)                |
|        │                                                                |
|        ▼ (Multi-pass resolution: Arity, Imports, Receivers, SCIP)       |
|   Resolved Knowledge Graph with 4-Tier Provenance:                      |
|        ├── exact  : Compiler type-checker proven (100% precision)       |
|        ├── high   : Unambiguous import + type discriminator (87-99%)   |
|        ├── medium : Multi-candidate heuristic lead (5-37%)              |
|        └── low    : Loose identifier match (Filtered out)               |
|        │                                                                |
|        ▼                                                                |
|   Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) Memory Graph (<250 MB RAM)                |
|        │                                                                |
|        ▼ (Sub-millisecond traversals)                                   |
|   Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server -> AI Agent (Cursor/Claude/etc.)  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### The Four Confidence Tiers

RepoCortex never lies about how much it knows. Every edge in the graph is tagged with its provenance:

| Confidence | Source | Typical Precision | What the Agent Does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `exact` | Compiler-backed SCIP indexers (`scip-go`, `scip-typescript`, etc.) | **100.0%** | Safe for automated refactoring, renames, and blocking CI gates. |
| `high` | Tree-Sitter AST with explicit package imports and receiver matching | **86.8% – 99.5%** | Reliable primary guidance for code exploration and planning. |
| `medium` | Multi-candidate type inference or package-level heuristics | **5.7% – 37.5%** | Treated as investigatory leads; never acted upon without verification. |
| `low` | Loose identifier matches across unrelated packages | **0.0% – 2.8%** | Filtered by default. Exposed only when explicitly requested. |

When an agent calls `cortex`, it doesn't get a vague similarity score. It gets:
> *"Symbol `SubmitOrder` reaches `ChargeCard` at Depth 2 (Confidence: `exact`, proven by compiler)."*

If an edge is heuristic (`medium`), RepoCortex attaches an advisory notice:
> *"Warning: Interface dispatch could not be proven at compile time. Verify candidates before modifying."*

---

## 4. Does Vector Search Have Any Role?

Honest engineering requires acknowledging trade-offs. Is vector search completely useless in software engineering?

No. Vector search and BM25 lexical search excel at **unstructured natural language discovery**:
- *"Where in this codebase do we calculate state sales tax?"*
- *"Find the configuration that controls retry backoff for Redis."*

In RepoCortex, we use full-text search (SQLite FTS5 BM25) for exactly that: **finding candidate entry points** from a user's natural language task prompt.

**Crucially, however, search is only the candidate finder. It is never the resolver.**
Once candidates are found, RepoCortex immediately projects them onto the deterministic graph:
1. Candidate nodes are validated against AST symbol definitions.
2. Unconnected noise (like marketing comments or logs) is pruned because it has zero graph degree to the rest of the system.
3. The true execution cluster is traversed along proven edges.
4. Only the connected, verified subgraph is emitted to the agent.

---

## 5. Summary: Why We Chose SQLite Over a Vector DB

| Dimension | Vector RAG | RepoCortex Deterministic Graph |
|---|---|---|
| **Underlying Math** | High-dimensional float cosine distance | Discrete relational graph algebra & AST traversals |
| **Edge Precision** | Uncalibrated probabilities (0.0 to 1.0) | Mathematically verified confidence tiers (`exact`, `high`, etc.) |
| **Transitive Blast Radius** | Impossible (Semantic similarity does not chain) | Sub-millisecond recursive walks with hub pruning |
| **Token Consumption** | 10k–30k tokens per query (raw file chunks) | 500–1,500 tokens per query (subgraph signatures) |
| **Storage & Dependencies** | Python service, vector DB, API keys, GPU | Single self-contained static binary, pure Go, local SQLite |
| **Privacy & Security** | Source code often sent to third-party embedding APIs | **100% offline**, zero telemetry, runs air-gapped on your laptop |
| **Refactoring Safety** | Hallucination hazard; unsafe for edits | Atomic rollback with multi-file AST validation |

We didn't build RepoCortex to jump on an AI hype cycle. We built it because software engineering is a discipline of precision. Your tools should be as rigorous as the code you write.


# --- END FILE: docs/WHY_NOT_VECTOR_RAG.md ---



# --- BEGIN FILE: docs/USER_GUIDE.md ---

# RepoCortex User Guide: The Enterprise Guide to Code Intelligence & Change Safety

RepoCortex is a local-first, zero-CGO code intelligence engine and knowledge graph for engineering teams and AI coding agents. It indexes large polyglot codebases into a queryable graph of symbols, call chains, HTTP endpoints, database access patterns, event broker queues, and test coverage—delivering deterministic answers over CLI, MCP (Model Context Protocol), and an embedded interactive portal.

---

## 1. Design Philosophy

Modern codebases suffer from context fragmentation. AI coding agents burn 80% of their token budget and reasoning time repeatedly grepping files, attempting to reconstruct architectural boundaries and tracing caller chains from scratch.

RepoCortex replaces speculative text search with deterministic graph intelligence:

1. **Every Fact Carries Provenance**: RepoCortex never conflates a compiler-proven fact with a heuristic regex match. All relationships carry confidence tiers (`exact`, `high`, `medium`, `low`).
2. **Zero-CGO & Local-First**: Written in pure Go using pure-Go SQLite (`modernc.org/sqlite`). It compiles to a self-contained static binary. Your proprietary source code never leaves your workstation or CI runner.
3. **Zero External LLM Calls in Core Engine**: Graph construction, BM25 indexing, AST pruning, and impact analysis run deterministically at native CPU speed with zero cloud API dependencies.
4. **Honest Incompleteness**: An empty query result distinguishes between "we proved this has no callers" and "this code has unresolvable dynamic references." Blind spots and omitted edges are reported explicitly.

---

## 2. Confidence Tier & Provenance Model

RepoCortex categorizes all graph relationships into four immutable tiers:

| Tier | Source | Typical Precision | Recommended Usage |
|---|---|---|---|
| `exact` | Compiler-backed SCIP indexers (`scip-go`, `scip-typescript`, `scip-python`, `scip-java`) | **100.0%** (Proved by compiler typechecker) | Fully automated refactoring and blocking CI gates. |
| `high` | Tree-sitter explicit import matching + unambiguous type discriminator | **86.8% – 99.5%** | Primary guidance for AI agents and human reviews. |
| `medium` | Multi-candidate type inference or package-level heuristic | **5.7% – 37.5%** | Displayed as informative leads; never acted on automatically. |
| `low` | Loose identifier name match across files | **0.0% – 2.8%** | Filtered out by default; accessible via `--min-confidence low`. |

To inspect your repository's measured precision and recall against your local toolchains:
```bash
cortex accuracy
```

---

## 3. Installation & Getting Started

### Pre-built Binary Installation

**macOS / Linux:**
```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/satyendrakumarsingh/cortex/main/install.sh | sh
```

**Windows (PowerShell):**
```powershell
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri https://raw.githubusercontent.com/satyendrakumarsingh/cortex/main/install.ps1 -OutFile install.ps1
.\install.ps1
```

### Building From Source (Go 1.25+)
```bash
git clone https://github.com/satyendrakumarsingh/cortex.git
cd cortex
go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o cortex ./cmd/cortex
sudo mv cortex /usr/local/bin/
```

### Initializing a Project

From the root of your git repository:
```bash
# 1. Initialize local configuration (.cortex.yml)
cortex init

# 2. Build the structural index (scans source files and extracts definitions)
cortex index

# 3. Resolve cross-file references and build the call graph
cortex resolve

# 4. Verify graph integrity
cortex doctor
```

Subsequent indexing runs are incremental: RepoCortex stores SHA-256 content hashes of files and re-indexes only files modified since the last run.

---

## 4. CLI Reference & Key Capabilities

### 4.1. Distributed Event Topology (`cortex events`)

RepoCortex statically tracks asynchronous event producers and consumers across distributed message brokers:
- **Supported Brokers**: Apache Kafka (Sarama, kafka-go, Spring Kafka, KafkaJS, kafka-python), RabbitMQ / AMQP, AWS SQS / SNS, and Google Cloud Pub/Sub.

```bash
# List all discovered topics/queues across the repository
cortex events

# Inspect producers and consumers for a specific topic
cortex events topic payment.settled

# Output machine-readable JSON
cortex events --json
```

Example human output:
```text
Event Topology Report (3 topics discovered)

Topic: payment.settled [kafka]
  Producers:
    - SettlementService.Finalize (services/settlement.go:142) [high]
  Consumers:
    - LedgerWorker.OnMessage (workers/ledger.go:88) [high]
    - NotificationHandler.HandleEvent (handlers/notify.ts:45) [high]
```

### 4.2. Code Blindspots & Missed References (`cortex missed`)

Static analysis frequently encounters dynamic dispatch, unmapped HTTP routes, orphan database tables, or critical paths lacking tests. `cortex missed` surfaces these blindspots before they cause production defects.

```bash
# Run a blindspot audit across the repository
cortex missed

# Output formatted JSON for custom CI/CD parsing
cortex missed --json
```

Discovered categories:
- `unresolved_call`: Dynamic or reflection-based calls where the target symbol could not be proven.
- `untested_critical`: Public API endpoints or database writers lacking covering test edges.
- `unmapped_endpoint`: Route handlers defined in code without client callers or framework contracts.
- `orphan_table`: Database tables defined in schemas or migrations with zero code readers or writers.

### 4.3. Deterministic Refactoring Plans (`cortex plan-change`)

Before refactoring a symbol or renaming a core function, `cortex plan-change` constructs an ordered, multi-step execution plan containing direct callers, affected tests, preconditions, and postconditions.

```bash
# Generate refactoring execution plan for a symbol
cortex plan-change --symbol ProcessRefund

# Output JSON plan for automated agent execution
cortex plan-change --symbol ProcessRefund --json
```

Example output:
```text
Refactor Plan for ProcessRefund (services/billing.go:112)
Risk Level: MEDIUM (Risk Score: 42/100)
Direct Callers: 4 | Affected Tests: 2

Preconditions:
  - Working directory is clean (no uncommitted edits)
  - Target symbol exists and compiles

Step 1 [update_caller]: Update call site in handlers/payment.go:64
Step 2 [update_caller]: Update call site in workers/retry.go:102
Step 3 [update_def]: Refactor signature in services/billing.go:112
Step 4 [verify_test]: Run covering test TestProcessRefundSuccess (services/billing_test.go:40)

Postconditions:
  - Run cortex doctor to ensure zero dangling reference edges
  - Run affected test suite
```

### 4.4. AST Interface Pruning (`cortex prune`)

When AI agents read source files, up to 90% of tokens are consumed by implementation logic inside method bodies. `cortex prune` parses Go, Python, and TypeScript/JavaScript files and strips all function bodies, replacing them with concise stubs while preserving all type signatures, struct fields, interfaces, and docstrings.

```bash
# Print pruned AST interface to stdout
cortex prune internal/store/sqlite.go

# Reduces a 1,200-line file (~12,000 tokens) to a 90-line interface (~900 tokens)
```

### 4.5. Token-Efficient Diff Minimization (`cortex diff-minimize`)

Standard git diffs contain excess context lines, whitespace noise, and redundant index headers. `cortex diff-minimize` parses patch streams into structured, token-efficient representations highlighting exact additions, removals, and symbol contexts.

```bash
git diff HEAD~1 | cortex diff-minimize
```

### 4.6. Task Context & Relevance Ranking (`cortex context`)

Given a natural language task description, RepoCortex uses BM25 full-text scoring combined with AST dependency graph traversal to locate the exact transitive file set required for the task.

```bash
cortex context "Add idempotency key validation to payment callback handler"
```

The context engine bridges domain concepts deterministically (e.g. mapping "credential leakage" to `redact.go` and `credentials_test.go`) without hallucination.

### 4.7. The Change-Safety Gate: Compile & Verify

RepoCortex enforces architecture rules and prevents regressions through a two-phase contract:

1. **Compile**: Convert an engineering intent into a strict JSON contract:
   ```bash
   cortex compile "Refactor auth middleware to use JWT tokens" --json > task-contract.json
   ```
2. **Work**: Engineer or AI agent makes changes.
3. **Verify**: Evaluate git changes against the contract:
   ```bash
   cortex verify --contract task-contract.json --changed "$(git diff --name-only | paste -sd, -)"
   ```

Exit Codes:
- `0` (`pass`): All checks satisfied with zero violations.
- `0` (`advisory`): Only heuristic leads discovered (use `--fail-on-leads` to reject).
- `1` (`fail`): At least one compiler-proven fact violation detected (e.g., breaking an architecture boundary or modifying an excluded file).
- `2` (`unverified`): No index or contract data available to verify.

### 4.8. Applying a Rename (`cortex rename`)

`plan-change` tells you what a rename touches; `rename` makes the edit, but only
where it can prove every site.

1. **Dry run first** (the default). It lists every site with its confidence and
   every site that would block an apply:
   ```bash
   cortex rename updateStatus applyStatus
   ```
2. **What blocks `--apply`.** It writes nothing, lists every failing site and
   exits `2` unless every site is `exact` (compiler-proven), unchanged since
   indexing, unambiguous on its line, inside the project root and writable, and
   the new name is not already defined in an edited file. On a project with no
   compiler index, every site is `high` and the rename is refused. Run
   `cortex indexers install --yes` and `cortex scip import` to upgrade them
   to `exact`.
3. **Opting into `high`.** `--floor high` also accepts an explicit import plus an
   unambiguous receiver type. That tier is measured 86.8-96.1% precise, so the
   command prints a warning first: at 90%, a rename touching thirty sites gets
   three wrong. Read every listed site.
   ```bash
   cortex rename updateStatus applyStatus --floor high --apply
   ```
4. **What `--apply` does.** Files are written atomically and restored if a later
   write fails. A lock file, `.cortex-edit.lock`, exists at the project root
   only while the edit runs; if a crashed run left it behind, RepoCortex never
   deletes it for you, and the error tells you to remove it once no cortex
   process is running. Then the task contract lands in
   `.cortex/rename-contract.json` and `verify` runs automatically on the
   changed files. `verify` reads the **pre-rename index**, so run
   `cortex index` afterwards.
5. **Exit codes.** `0` applied and verified; `1` error or verify failure; `2`
   refused, nothing written; `3` applied, but not verified complete: either
   `verify` was unverified, or the old name still appears in indexed files, which
   are listed under `LEFTOVER OCCURRENCES`. Handle them by hand.
6. **RepoCortex does not run the compiler.** References it could not bind, and
   interface implementations or overrides with no edge to the symbol, are not
   renamed. After every rename, search for the old name, then **build and
   test**.

---

---

## 5. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server Setup

RepoCortex includes a built-in MCP server that communicates over JSON-RPC via standard input/output.

### Claude Desktop Configuration
Add RepoCortex to `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`:
```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "cortex": {
      "command": "cortex",
      "args": ["serve", "--project", "/path/to/your/repository"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Cursor & Windsurf Configuration
In Cursor or Windsurf MCP Settings:
- **Name**: `cortex`
- **Type**: `command`
- **Command**: `cortex serve --project /path/to/your/repository`

### Available MCP Tools

AI agents connected to RepoCortex gain access to:
- `get_project_overview`: Orient on the repository: languages, size, resolution coverage.
- `search_code` / `find_symbol` / `get_symbol`: Locate declarations with exact file, line, and kind.
- `find_callers` / `find_references`: Retrieve incoming call edges and usage sites with confidence grades.
- `get_task_context`: Obtain ranked file summaries and symbol graphs for a prompt.
- `impact_analysis`: Calculate transitive impact (blast radius) and risk for a change.
- `find_tests`: Find the tests that cover a symbol or file.
- `plan_change`: Generate a step-by-step refactoring plan with preconditions and post-checks.
- `plan_rename`: Enumerate every site a rename must touch.
- `detect_blindspots`: Audit unresolved calls, unmapped endpoints, orphan tables and missing config.
- `get_file_outline`: Obtain a token-optimized outline (signatures, types, docs; bodies pruned) of a file.
- `minimize_diff`: Compress unified git diffs into structured, token-efficient patch contexts.
- `find_api_endpoints` / `find_db_access` / `get_config_key`: Query HTTP endpoints, database access and configuration keys.
- `resolution_coverage`: Report how much of the call graph is resolved, so an empty result is not over-trusted.

Some tools need the `standard` profile; see [agent-integration.md](agent-integration.md).
Event topology (`cortex events`) is available from the CLI and the portal, not as an MCP tool.

---

## 6. Enterprise Interactive Dashboard (`cortex ui`)

RepoCortex includes an embedded, high-performance web dashboard providing complete $N$-level visibility into your codebase architecture.

To launch the portal:
```bash
cortex ui
```
By default, the server listens on loopback (`127.0.0.1`) on an ephemeral port and prints the access URL.

### Command Palette (`Cmd+K` / `Ctrl+K`)
Press `Cmd+K` (macOS) or `Ctrl+K` (Linux/Windows) anywhere in the portal to open the global Command Palette:
- Instant fuzzy navigation to any screen (`Overview`, `Explore Graph`, `APIs`, `Database`, `Events`, `Blindspots`, `Plan Refactor`, `Governance`, `Metrics`).
- Quick actions: reload data, copy repo root, trigger index refresh.

### 360° Symbol Inspector Drawer
Clicking any symbol name anywhere in the application (in tables, graph nodes, callers, or refactor steps) slides open the 360° Symbol Inspector drawer from the right:
- Definition path and exact line number with one-click editor opening (`vscode://`).
- Inbound callers and outbound dependencies grouped by confidence.
- Database read/write associations and event broker linkages.
- Covering tests and test gap analysis.

### Screens Overview
- **System Overview**: High-level repository health, language breakdown, resolution coverage rate, and freshness indicators.
- **Code map** — four views of the index behind one breadcrumb and one tab strip. They share the selection, so a symbol chosen in one view is selected in the others:
  - **Graph**: the canvas map of directories, files or symbols, with grouping, focus, path finding and three layouts.
  - **Tree**: the repository as an outline, directory → file → symbol, navigable with the keyboard.
  - **Treemap**: where the code is — boxes sized by symbols and coloured by connections, exported share or language.
  - **Code**: a file's text as the index holds it, with its declarations, callers and callees, and the lines relationships cite. Served by `GET /api/source` from the index's own copy, never from disk.
- **Event Bus & Queues**: Interactive topology of Kafka topics, AMQP exchanges, and cloud pub/sub queues with publisher and consumer cards.
- **Code Blindspots**: Actionable matrix of unmapped endpoints, unresolved dynamic calls, and orphan database tables with remediation suggestions.
- **Plan a Refactor**: Interactive refactoring orchestrator generating step-by-step modification lists with preconditions, affected tests, and post-checks.
- **Architecture Governance**: Real-time evaluation of declared Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) and prohibited dependency boundaries.

---

## 7. CI/CD Integration: GitHub Actions Change-Safety Gate

RepoCortex can be integrated directly into your GitHub Actions workflow to fail pull requests that introduce architecture violations or high-severity blindspots (`--fail-on`, default `high`), and to publish what it found: a sticky pull-request comment, code-scanning alerts (SARIF) and the job summary. Reports are published before the gate runs, so a failing build still leaves the reviewer a comment and alerts that explain why.

Create `.github/workflows/cortex-gate.yml` (the repository ships this exact file):
```yaml
name: RepoCortex Change-Safety Gate

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

env:
  # Lowest blindspot / architecture severity that fails the build: high|medium|low.
  CORTEX_FAIL_ON: high
  # auto: install the pinned compiler-backed indexers this repository needs and
  # import their facts as `exact` before impact runs. fast: skip that stage; the
  # report stays heuristic and says so.
  CORTEX_ACCURACY: auto

jobs:
  gate:
    name: Change-Safety Verification
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write   # the sticky report comment
      security-events: write # SARIF upload to code scanning
    steps:
      - name: Checkout Repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Setup Go Environment
        id: setup-go
        uses: actions/setup-go@v5
        with:
          go-version: '1.25.x'
          cache: true

      - name: Build RepoCortex
        run: go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o ./bin/cortex ./cmd/cortex

      # resolve is not optional: without it the index holds definitions but no
      # call graph, and every impact and blindspot result below would be empty
      # for the wrong reason.
      - name: Index and Resolve
        run: |
          ./bin/cortex index
          ./bin/cortex resolve

      # The cache key is the pin table itself, so it changes exactly when a
      # pinned version or digest does.
      - name: Pin Compiler Indexers
        if: env.CORTEX_ACCURACY == 'auto'
        run: |
          mkdir -p cortex-out
          ./bin/cortex indexers pins > cortex-out/indexer-pins.txt

      # Only scip-go is cached: it is built by `go install` into GOPATH/bin,
      # which setup-go puts on PATH. npm and container indexers are fetched and
      # digest-verified on every run.
      - name: Cache Compiler Indexers
        if: env.CORTEX_ACCURACY == 'auto'
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/go/bin/scip-go
          key: cortex-indexers-${{ runner.os }}-go${{ steps.setup-go.outputs.go-version }}-${{ hashFiles('cortex-out/indexer-pins.txt') }}

      # An accuracy upgrade, never a requirement: if an indexer is missing, blocked
      # or produces an index that will not import, the edges stay heuristic and the
      # report says so. A language whose toolchain is missing is skipped with its
      # reason (kept in cortex-out/indexers.txt and the step summary). Java is
      # never built here: without the repo-build opt-in its indexer is reported as
      # blocked.
      - name: Import Compiler Facts
        if: env.CORTEX_ACCURACY == 'auto'
        run: |
          mkdir -p cortex-out
          { ./bin/cortex indexers install --yes --out-dir cortex-out/scip 2>&1 \
              || echo "::warning::compiler indexers unavailable; the report uses heuristic edges"; } \
            | tee cortex-out/indexers.txt
          imported=0
          failed=0
          for f in cortex-out/scip/*.scip; do
            [ -f "$f" ] || continue
            if ./bin/cortex scip import "$f"; then
              imported=$((imported + 1))
            else
              echo "::warning::scip import of $(basename "$f") failed; its edges stay heuristic"
              failed=$((failed + 1))
            fi
          done
          {
            echo "### Compiler-backed precision"
            echo "imported: $imported, failed: $failed"
            echo '```'
            cat cortex-out/indexers.txt
            echo '```'
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

      - name: Verify Index Integrity
        run: ./bin/cortex doctor --verify-index

      # Reports are collected and published BEFORE the gate runs, so a failing
      # gate still leaves the reviewer a comment and code-scanning alerts that
      # say why.
      - name: Collect Findings
        run: |
          mkdir -p cortex-out
          ./bin/cortex --json arch > cortex-out/arch.json
          ./bin/cortex --json missed > cortex-out/missed.json

      - name: Impact Analysis of the Pull Request
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
        run: ./bin/cortex --json impact --base "origin/${{ github.base_ref }}" --head HEAD > cortex-out/impact.json

      - name: Render Reports
        run: |
          ./bin/cortex report sarif --arch cortex-out/arch.json --missed cortex-out/missed.json --out cortex-out/cortex.sarif
          if [ -f cortex-out/impact.json ]; then
            ./bin/cortex report pr --impact cortex-out/impact.json --arch cortex-out/arch.json --missed cortex-out/missed.json --out cortex-out/pr-report.md
          else
            ./bin/cortex report pr --arch cortex-out/arch.json --missed cortex-out/missed.json --out cortex-out/pr-report.md
          fi
          cat cortex-out/pr-report.md >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

      # A fork pull request's token is read-only and cannot write security
      # events; the PR comment and step summary still carry the findings.
      - name: Upload SARIF to Code Scanning
        if: github.event_name == 'push' || github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        with:
          sarif_file: cortex-out/cortex.sarif
          category: cortex

      # Same-repository pull requests only: a fork's token cannot write
      # comments, and this job never runs fork code with write permissions.
      - name: Post Sticky PR Comment
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request' && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
          PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
        run: |
          id=$(gh api "repos/$REPO/issues/$PR/comments" --paginate \
            --jq '.[] | select(.body | contains("<!-- cortex:pr-report -->")) | .id' | head -n 1)
          if [ -n "$id" ]; then
            gh api -X PATCH "repos/$REPO/issues/comments/$id" -F body=@cortex-out/pr-report.md
          else
            gh api -X POST "repos/$REPO/issues/$PR/comments" -F body=@cortex-out/pr-report.md
          fi

      - name: Report Event Topology
        run: ./bin/cortex events

      - name: Enforce Architecture Rules
        run: ./bin/cortex arch --fail-on "$CORTEX_FAIL_ON"

      - name: Audit Code Blindspots
        run: ./bin/cortex missed --fail-on "$CORTEX_FAIL_ON"
```

The `Collect Findings` step saves `cortex --json arch|missed|impact` output; `cortex report sarif` turns it into a SARIF 2.1.0 file uploaded to code scanning under the category `cortex`, and `cortex report pr` renders one bounded Markdown comment that starts with `<!-- cortex:pr-report -->`. That marker is how the workflow finds and edits its own comment on later pushes instead of adding a new one. The job needs `pull-requests: write` (the comment) and `security-events: write` (the SARIF upload); the workflow sets both on the job only. Pull requests from forks get neither the comment nor the code-scanning upload, because a fork's token is read-only; they still get the job summary and the gate. The blast-radius analysis runs only on pull requests, and none of the reporting steps fail the build -- the `Enforce` steps at the end do.

**Compiler-backed precision.** With `CORTEX_ACCURACY: auto` (the default) the gate runs `cortex indexers install --yes --out-dir cortex-out/scip` after `resolve`, then `cortex scip import` on every index it produced, so `impact` walks compiler-proven `exact` edges wherever a compiler exists. `--yes` is the CI operator's consent to install the pinned indexers listed by `cortex indexers pins`; nothing else is installed, and every download is pinned and verified (by digest, or by the Go checksum database for scip-go). The runner needs the language's own toolchain — Go for scip-go (setup-go provides it), Node for scip-typescript and scip-python; a project whose toolchain is missing is skipped with its reason. Java is never built by this workflow. The stage is an accuracy upgrade, never a requirement, and it never fails the job: if an indexer is missing, blocked, or produces an index that will not import, the gate emits a `::warning::`, the edges stay heuristic, and the job summary gains a "Compiler-backed precision" section listing the imported and failed counts and each skipped language with its reason. scip-go is cached under a key derived from the pin table. Set `CORTEX_ACCURACY: fast` to skip the stage; the PR report then shows, in a "How much of the blast radius is proven" table, what share of the blast radius is `exact`, `high` and `medium` (interface-dispatch-only symbols are not counted). The step never passes `--allow-repo-build`, so fork pull requests, which run with a read-only token, execute only pinned, digest-verified indexers and never the repository's own build.

---

## 8. Summary & Best Practices

1. **Keep the Index Fresh**: Add `cortex hooks install` to your development environment to automatically refresh the index on every git commit in 20 milliseconds without running background daemons.
2. **Import Compiler Data in CI**: Place the compiler's `index.scip` in the project root (or `.cortex/`) before `cortex resolve`, which imports it automatically (`--no-scip` opts out), or run `cortex scip import` yourself, to upgrade heuristic edges to compiler-backed `exact` confidence.
3. **Trust `exact` and `high`, Verify `medium`**: Never allow AI coding agents or automated scripts to execute destructive refactoring operations on `medium` or `low` confidence edges without explicit human review.

---

## 9. Comprehensive Product Capabilities

RepoCortex delivers an end-to-end change-safety and code intelligence architecture. The following matrix details each capability and its operational mechanism:

### 9.1. Polyglot AST Precision Engine & Arity Dialects
- **Multi-Language Parsing**: Zero-external-dependency Tree-Sitter grammars compiled directly into pure Go. Supports Go, TypeScript, JavaScript, Java, Python, C#, Rust, C, C++, and Ruby.
- **Arity & Overload Resolution**: Parameter count queries (`paramCountQueries`) and call argument queries (`argCountQueries`) distinguish methods overloaded by parameter count in Java, C#, and TypeScript.
- **Dynamic Arena Memory Management**: Automatically triggers parser pool memory draining upon encountering large generated files (>256 KiB), eliminating multi-gigabyte heap spikes during repository batch scans.

### 9.2. Change Safety & Blast Radius Analytics (`cortex impact`, `cortex plan-change`)
- **Upstream & Downstream Traversal**: Answers both *"what does this function call?"* (downstream dependencies) and *"what in the entire enterprise depends on this function?"* (upstream blast radius).
- **Hub Pruning**: Automatically prunes traversals across high-degree utility nodes (such as loggers, string formatters, and base object classes) to avoid exponential combinatorial explosions while explicitly reporting the cutoff boundary.
- **Test Gap Detection (`cortex missed`)**: Proves whether modified code paths have verified test coverage or whether execution branches are blind to the testing suite.

### 9.3. Safe Automated Refactoring (`cortex rename`)
- **Exact AST Identifier Splicing**: Matches identifiers strictly on AST node boundaries. Never confuses a symbol name with a comment, string literal, or substring token.
- **Reversible Multi-File Rollback**: Takes an in-memory snapshot before modifying source code. If any file write fails or post-apply verification detects an orphaned call site, RepoCortex rolls back all files across the repository to their original state in reverse order.
- **Leftover Occurrence Scanning**: Audits all files (including unindexed or binary files) post-rename to ensure no stale references to the old symbol persist.

### 9.4. Architecture Governance & CI/CD Gates (`cortex arch`)
- **Structural Boundary Enforcement**: Declaratively defines allowed import and call relationships between architectural layers (e.g. `domain` must never import `infrastructure` or `controller`).
- **PR Gating & SARIF 2.1.0**: Generates standard SARIF code-scanning artifacts and sticky GitHub PR comments showing exact change risk and architectural compliance scores.

### 9.5. Cross-Stack Distributed Topology (`cortex api`, `cortex db`, `cortex events`)
- **HTTP / REST Endpoints**: Statically discovers route handlers across Express, Spring Boot, Gin, FastAPI, NestJS, and ASP.NET.
- **Database Access Maps**: Maps database tables, ORM models (Prisma, GORM, Hibernate, SQLAlchemy), and raw SQL queries to identifying calling methods.
- **Distributed Event Topologies**: Extracts producer and consumer queues across Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, AWS SQS/SNS, and Google Cloud Pub/Sub.

### 9.6. AI Coding Agent MCP Server (`cortex serve`, `cortex install`)
- **Compact Subgraph Extraction**: Delivers targeted subgraphs and pruned signatures instead of raw file dumps, saving up to 85% of LLM token windows.
- **Confidence Advisory Notices**: Automatically attaches warning notes when query results contain heuristic (`medium` or `low`) edges, preventing autonomous agents from acting on hallucinatory call chains.

---

## 10. Deep Comparative Analysis: RepoCortex vs Alternative Tools

Rather than evaluating specific vendor brands, the following analysis benchmarks RepoCortex against the primary architectural classes of code intelligence and developer tools currently deployed in the software industry:

```
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                  TOOL CATEGORY COMPARISON OVERVIEW                               |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| RepoCortex                  : Pure-Go static binary, deterministic graph, safe transactional edits |
| Category A (LSP Daemons)  : Per-language server silos, heavy memory, navigation only, no cross-db|
| Category B (Vector RAG)   : Fuzzy text embeddings, 80%+ hallucinations, massive token waste      |
| Category C (Heavy SAST)   : Multi-hour batch scans, alert fatigue, read-only, non-agent-native   |
| Category D (Text Greppers): High speed, zero semantic awareness, false-positive substring matches|
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### Detailed Evaluation by Tool Category

#### Category 1: Traditional Language Server Protocol (LSP) Daemons
* **How They Work**: Run language-specific daemons (e.g., `gopls`, `tsserver`, `jdtls`) in the background of an IDE to provide real-time auto-complete and go-to-definition.
* **Limitations Compared to RepoCortex**:
  - **Siloed by Language**: An LSP cannot connect a TypeScript frontend API call to a Java Spring Boot endpoint, nor can it trace a Go publisher to a Python Kafka consumer.
  - **Resource Heavy**: Running 3 to 4 distinct language servers in a microservice monorepo easily consumes 4–8 GB of RAM.
  - **No Global Change Impact**: LSPs provide local symbol lookups but lack graph traversal capabilities (e.g., multi-hop blast radius, hub pruning, test gap discovery).
* **Where RepoCortex Excels**: RepoCortex unifies all languages into a single SQLite knowledge graph running in a single lightweight process with flat memory footprint.

#### Category 2: Naive Vector Search / Embedding-Based Code RAG
*(For an exhaustive architectural essay, see [Why Vector RAG Fails for Code: The Case for Deterministic Graph Intelligence](WHY_NOT_VECTOR_RAG.md))*
* **How They Work**: Chunk source code into text windows, compute dense vector embeddings, and perform cosine similarity searches to retrieve context for LLMs.
* **Limitations Compared to RepoCortex**:
  - **Fuzzy Guesswork vs Deterministic Truth**: Vector similarity finds code that *reads similarly*, not code that is *actually executed*. A method named `processPayment` will match unrelated payment helpers while missing the actual interface implementation `settle`.
  - **Extreme Token Waste**: Dumping entire source files or arbitrary chunks into an LLM context consumes tens of thousands of tokens per prompt, leading to high cost and lost-in-the-middle context degradation.
  - **Zero Safety Guarantees**: Vector search provides zero safety invariants for automated refactoring or architecture governance.
* **Where RepoCortex Excels**: RepoCortex delivers exact call graphs and pruned signatures, reducing prompt token consumption by up to 85% while providing mathematically calibrated confidence tiers.

#### Category 3: Heavyweight Enterprise Static Analysis (SAST) Suites
* **How They Work**: Execute deep interprocedural taint analysis and abstract interpretation to detect security vulnerabilities and code quality flaws.
* **Limitations Compared to RepoCortex**:
  - **Hours-Long Execution**: Full repository scans take 30 minutes to several hours, preventing interactive developer use.
  - **High False-Positive Noise**: Developers frequently suffer from alert fatigue due to uncalibrated heuristic warnings.
  - **Read-Only / Non-Agent Native**: Designed for compliance reporting rather than active pair-programming with AI coding agents.
* **Where RepoCortex Excels**: RepoCortex indexes 10,000 files in seconds, provides sub-millisecond query latency via in-memory CSR graphs, and integrates natively into agent workflows via standard MCP tools.

#### Category 4: Static LSIF / SCIP Compiler-Only Dumpers
* **How They Work**: Compile code using full toolchains (`scip-go`, `scip-typescript`) and write large protocol buffer files storing cross-references.
* **Limitations Compared to RepoCortex**:
  - **Brittle Setup Requirements**: Require every compiler, SDK, private registry credential, and native dependency to be fully configured on the host. If a build fails, zero index is produced.
  - **Static / Non-Queryable**: Output static dump files that cannot be dynamically traversed, queried for blast radius, or updated incrementally on file save.
* **Where RepoCortex Excels**: RepoCortex provides zero-setup Tree-Sitter heuristic indexing out of the box, with optional seamless SCIP compiler enrichment (`cortex scip import`). If a compiler is missing, RepoCortex still delivers an 87%+ accurate graph.

#### Category 5: Fast Regex / Text Greppers (ripgrep, ag, ctags)
* **How They Work**: Execute optimized parallel string and regular expression searches across file trees.
* **Limitations Compared to RepoCortex**:
  - **No Semantic Awareness**: Cannot distinguish between a function definition, an invocation, a comment, a string literal, or a substring in an unrelated variable name.
  - **No Graph Traversability**: Cannot trace multi-hop call hierarchies, dependency chains, or transitive blast radius.
* **Where RepoCortex Excels**: RepoCortex understands AST node boundaries, receiver types, and call semantics.

---

### Comprehensive Capabilities & Architectural Comparison Matrix

| Architectural Feature | RepoCortex | Traditional LSP Daemons | Vector Embedding RAG | Enterprise SAST Suites | Static SCIP / LSIF Dumpers | Text Greppers (`rg`) |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Zero-Setup Polyglot Indexing** | **Yes** (Native Go) | No (Per-language SDKs) | Yes (Raw text) | No (Complex setups) | No (Full build required) | **Yes** |
| **Deterministic Call Graphs** | **Yes** | Yes (Single language) | No (Fuzzy similarity) | Yes | **Yes** | No (String match) |
| **Cross-Stack Topologies (DB/API/Events)** | **Yes** | No | No | Partial (Security only) | No | No |
| **Calibrated Confidence Provenance** | **Yes** (4 Tiers) | Implicit (Uncalibrated) | No (Distance metric) | No (Severity, not truth) | **Yes** (Compiler-only) | No |
| **Transitive Blast Radius (`impact`)** | **Yes** (With Hub Pruning)| No | No | No | No | No |
| **AI Agent MCP Server Native** | **Yes** (10+ tools) | No | Partial (Retrieval only)| No | No | No |
| **Atomic Multi-File Safe Refactoring** | **Yes** (With Rollback) | Partial (LSP rename) | No | No | No | No (Blind replace) |
| **Incremental File Watch Latency** | **<50 ms** | <100 ms | Seconds to minutes | Hours (Batch only) | Batch only | Instant (Stateless) |
| **Memory Footprint on 10K Files** | **<250 MB** | 2–6 GB | 1–3 GB + Vector DB | 4–16 GB | N/A (Static file) | **<50 MB** |
| **100% Offline / Air-Gapped Operation** | **Yes** | **Yes** | No (Often needs cloud) | Often Cloud-hosted | **Yes** | **Yes** |
| **Single Standalone Static Binary** | **Yes** (Zero CGO) | No | No | No | No | **Yes** |


# --- END FILE: docs/USER_GUIDE.md ---



# --- BEGIN FILE: docs/agent-integration.md ---

# Agent integration

RepoCortex is a server. Wiring it up has two halves, and only one of them is the
MCP registration.

The other half is guidance. An agent with the tools connected but nothing
telling it *when* to reach for them will keep grepping, because a tool
description is only read once the agent has already decided to look at the tool
list. Nothing in a tool schema can say "before you edit a symbol, ask for its
blast radius first". That sentence has to live in project memory.

Both halves come out of one command:

```
cortex agent
```

---

## 1. Register the MCP server

### Claude Code, one line

```
claude mcp add cortex -- cortex --project /path/to/repo serve
```

`--project` is explicit on purpose. An MCP client starts the server from
whatever directory it happens to be in, and a server that quietly indexed the
wrong repository would be worse than one that failed to start.

`cortex agent` prints this line with your project's real path substituted, so
you can paste it rather than editing it.

### Claude Code, as a plugin

This repository ships a plugin manifest at `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`. It
registers the same MCP server *and* installs the guidance as a skill, so one
step delivers both halves:

```
claude --plugin-dir /path/to/cortex
```

`--plugin-dir` loads a plugin straight from a directory, without installing it.
To install it properly, or to hand it to a team, add the repository as a
marketplace — `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` is there for that:

```
/plugin marketplace add /path/to/cortex
/plugin install cortex@cortex
```

The manifest pins the project root with `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}`, which Claude
Code expands to the project you have open:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "cortex": {
      "command": "cortex",
      "args": ["--project", "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}", "serve"]
    }
  }
}
```

The plugin does **not** ship the `cortex` binary. Build or install it first
and make sure it is on `PATH`.

### Any other MCP client

RepoCortex speaks MCP over stdio. Whatever config format your client uses, these
are the three facts it needs:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| transport | stdio |
| command | `cortex` |
| args | `--project /path/to/repo serve` |

For a client that reads the common `mcpServers` JSON shape — including a
project-scope `.mcp.json` in the repository root:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "cortex": {
      "command": "cortex",
      "args": ["--project", "/path/to/repo", "serve"]
    }
  }
}
```

`cortex agent --json` emits the same spec as machine-readable JSON, if you
would rather generate the config than write it.

---

## 2. Give the agent the guidance

```
cortex agent --guidance >> CLAUDE.md
```

That appends a short block, delimited by `<!-- cortex:guidance -->` markers,
that tells the agent when to use each tool and how to read what comes back. It
is deliberately short: an agent skims project memory, and a page of prose is
ignored in exactly the same way as no prose at all.

`--guidance` prints the block and nothing else — no banner, no trailing advice —
because the output is meant to land in a file you keep.

If you would rather have it as its own file:

```
cortex agent --write docs/cortex-guidance.md
```

`--write` refuses to replace a file that already exists. Passing `--force`
allows it and says on stderr what it discarded. **No mode of this command
modifies your global configuration** — where the integration goes is your
decision, so the default is to print and let you place it.

### What the guidance actually says

Every rule is grounded in behaviour the server has, not in aspiration:

| Rule | Why it exists |
| --- | --- |
| Call `get_task_context` first | Its own description opens `CALL THIS FIRST`. One call replaces a dozen exploratory ones. |
| Ask for a blast radius before editing | `impact_analysis` on the `standard` profile, `find_callers` otherwise. |
| `find_tests` before changing behaviour | It reports *which signal* found each test — a proven call edge outranks a filename match. |
| Treat anything below `exact` as a lead | `exact` means a compiler proved it. `high`/`medium`/`low` were inferred and may be wrong. |
| An empty result means unresolved, not absent | Relationship answers are a lower bound. An agent told "no callers" will happily delete a live method. |
| `COVERAGE TOO LOW` outranks the list under it | The server emits that literal string when under half of the repository's references are bound. |
| "No index has been built" is not a broken tool | It is a recoverable state with a one-command fix, and the server deliberately returns it as a success. |
| The index is a snapshot, not your working tree | Read files you just edited directly, or run `cortex watch`. |

---

## 3. Check it landed

```
cortex agent --check
```

It reports six things, reading only — it never creates what it finds missing:

- **index** — present, committed, non-empty
- **resolution** — how much of the call graph is actually bound
- **mcp tools** — which profile is active and what it exposes
- **mcp registration** — whether this repository's `.mcp.json` names `cortex`
- **guidance** — whether `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md` carries the marker
- **plugin manifest** — whether `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` is present

Nothing missing is reported as a failure, and the command exits zero unless the
index is genuinely unreadable. An un-integrated project is the normal starting
state, not a malfunction — the same judgement the MCP server makes about
`isError`. Add `--json` to consume it from a script.

Note that `--check` sees the **project scope** only. A registration you added
with `claude mcp add` at user or local scope lives outside the repository, so it
is invisible here; the check says "not visible from this repository" rather than
claiming you have not registered it.

---

## What to expect once it is wired up

### The tool surface is small on purpose

```
$ cortex serve --list-tools
MCP profile "minimal" exposes 7 tool(s):
  get_project_overview
  search_code
  find_symbol
  get_symbol
  find_references
  find_callers
  get_task_context
```

Every exposed schema is injected into the agent's context on *every* request, so
a wide tool surface spends the very context RepoCortex exists to save — and a long
tool list measurably degrades tool selection. Seven is the default, and it is a
product decision rather than a limitation.

`impact_analysis` and `find_tests` need the `standard` profile. Set it in
`.cortex.yml`:

```yaml
mcp:
  profile: standard
```

```
$ cortex serve --list-tools
MCP profile "standard" exposes 9 tool(s):
  get_project_overview
  search_code
  find_symbol
  get_symbol
  find_references
  find_callers
  get_task_context
  impact_analysis
  find_tests
```

The guidance block adds **no tools**. It is text in project memory, paid for
once, that teaches the agent an ordering over the tools already there.

### There must be an index

The server refuses to start without one, and an empty index answers every
question with nothing:

```
cortex init
cortex index
cortex resolve
```

`resolve` is the step people skip. `index` extracts references but cannot bind
them — that needs the complete symbol table, which does not exist until every
file is parsed. Until `resolve` runs, `find_callers` and `find_references`
return nothing, and *nothing is the answer most easily mistaken for a fact*.
`cortex agent --check` calls this out as its own row for that reason.

### Answers carry their own caveats

RepoCortex does not hand an agent a tidy list built on evidence it does not have.
A relationship answer on a poorly resolved index arrives with the verdict
*before* the list:

```
COVERAGE TOO LOW — caller lookup for Go is unreliable here: 31% of this index's
16973 references are bound to a definition. Run 'cortex resolve' to raise it.
Do not present what follows as an answer to the question asked.
```

And a recoverable condition arrives as a **successful** call whose text says what
to do next, never as a tool error:

```
No index has been built for this project yet, so there is nothing to answer from.
Run 'cortex index' in the project root, then ask again. This is not a tool
failure: RepoCortex is working and the index is simply absent.
```

That distinction is load-bearing. A model that sees a tool fail early concludes
the toolset is broken and stops calling it for the rest of the session, so an
error is reserved for security refusals and genuine malfunction. The guidance
tells the agent to read these as instructions rather than as failures.

While the first index of a project is being built, the same mechanism answers
that the index is *still being built* (wait, and do not start a second one)
rather than "no index has been built". Once a run is committed, an answer taken
from it carries a note when a newer run is being built, because that answer may
not reflect recent edits.

---

## Keeping it current

The index describes the last committed run, not your working tree.

```
cortex watch      # re-index on change
cortex status     # revision, counts, resolution coverage
```

For files you edited moments ago, read them directly — the guidance says so, so
the agent will not report a stale definition as current.

---

## The CLI is the same engine

Every MCP tool has a command-line counterpart, which is the fastest way to see
*why* an agent received what it received:

```
cortex context "Add idempotency to payment callback processing"   # get_task_context, with exclusions
cortex callers <symbol>                                           # find_callers
cortex references <symbol>                                        # find_references
cortex symbol <name>                                              # find_symbol
cortex search <query>                                             # search_code
cortex status                                                     # get_project_overview
```

`cortex context --show-excluded` lists everything considered and left out with
the reason it was cut, which is the part an agent never shows you.


# --- END FILE: docs/agent-integration.md ---



# --- BEGIN FILE: docs/CLI.md ---

# CLI reference

One entry per command: the question it answers, its flags, one example that was
actually run, and the exit code where it is load-bearing. This is a lookup table.
For "which of these do I need", start at [GUIDE.md](GUIDE.md); for the reasoning
and the longer worked examples, [user-manual.md](user-manual.md).

Where a command's own `--help` argues its design, that argument is not repeated
here. Run `cortex <command> --help` — the help text in this tool is written to
be read.

## Global flags

Available on every command.

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--json` | emit machine-readable JSON on stdout |
| `--project <dir>` | project root (default: current directory) |
| `-q`, `--quiet` | suppress all logging |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | verbose logging |

Every query command takes `--json`. That is deliberate: a git hook or a CI check
should not have to speak JSON-RPC to ask the same questions the MCP tools answer.

## The provenance warning

Every index run records the build that wrote it. When a query command opens an
index written by a **different** build, it says so on stderr and then answers
anyway:

```
$ cortex callers Greet
time=… level=WARN msg="This index was written by cortex dev and you are running
9.9.9-test. Resolution rules change between builds, so these results may come from
different rules than this binary would produce. Re-index to refresh."
Greet (function) at main.go:3

KIND   SYMBOL  EVIDENCE   CONFIDENCE
CALLS  main    main.go:5  high (source_code)

1 caller(s).
```

An index is data *plus* the resolution rules that produced it, and those rules
have already changed twice in this project's history in ways that moved real
edges. An index written either side of such a change holds different edges for
identical source, and every query against it succeeds and looks exactly as
trustworthy as a current one. There is no symptom to notice, which is why the
index has to say so itself.

A run with no stamp — one written before the column existed — reports **unknown**
provenance rather than known staleness, because the advice differs: "re-index to
be sure" is not the same as "these results came from other rules".

Neither is an error. `-q` suppresses it along with all other logging. A schema
mismatch is a different thing and *is* an error, because the reader cannot
safely interpret the rows at all:

```
$ cortex callers Redact
error: index schema is v7 but this build of cortex expects v8 — run 'cortex index' to upgrade it
```

## Exit codes

Most commands are 0 on success and 1 on error. Four gate:

| Command | Codes |
|---|---|
| [`verify`](#verify) | 0 `pass`, 0 `advisory`, 1 `fail`, 2 `unverified` |
| [`arch --fail-on`](#arch) | 1 when a violation at or above that severity exists |
| [`bench --fail-on-regression`](#bench) | 1 when any case fails |
| [`docs --check`](#docs) | 1 when the committed documents have drifted |
| [`rename`](#rename-old-new) | 0 would apply, or applied with `verify` passing or advisory; 1 error, `verify` `fail`, or an incomplete rollback; 2 refused (nothing written); 3 applied but not verified complete |

---

## Index lifecycle

### `init`

**Answers:** nothing yet — it creates `.cortex/` and applies the registry
schema. It does not index.

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--force` | recreate the index if it already exists |

```
$ cortex init
Initialized RepoCortex for "payfix2"
  Index:          /path/payfix2/.cortex/index.db
  Schema version: 8 (8 migration(s) applied)
  Accuracy mode:  auto

Next: cortex index
```

### `index`

**Answers:** what is in this repository? Walks it, parses every supported file,
and makes the result queryable. Incremental by default — files are compared by
**content hash**, not mtime, so a `git checkout` does not trigger a full
reparse.

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--full` | rebuild from scratch. Discards resolved edges; re-run `resolve` |
| `--accuracy fast\|auto\|exact` | override the accuracy mode (full path only) |
| `--workers N` | parse concurrency (default 4). Peak memory scales with this, not with repository size |
| `--digest` | print the registry digest — the determinism gate |

`--workers` and `--accuracy` take effect only on the `--full` path, but are
validated on every path, so a typo fails immediately rather than being silently
discarded:

```
$ cortex index --accuracy nonsense
error: --accuracy "nonsense": want fast, auto or exact
$ echo $?
1
```

A full rebuild publishes atomically: the new revision becomes visible only once
the whole run is written, so an interrupted rebuild leaves the previous revision
in place.

```
$ cortex index --full --digest
  Files:         422 indexed, 54 skipped (476 discovered)
  Symbols:       6259
  References:    29506 (unresolved until M2)
  Imports:       2063
  Digest:        74f82dd64551014cbaad1be87228d2ac720c7ac0ca49ccfd856eb0bfe4a5d54b
  Duration:      7346ms
```

### `resolve`

**Answers:** which definition does each reference point at? Builds the call
graph. Separate from `index` because binding needs the complete symbol table,
which does not exist until every file has been parsed.

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--min-confidence high\|medium\|low` | drop bindings weaker than this instead of recording them |
| `--no-scip` | do not import an `index.scip` found in the project root or `.cortex/` |

Resolution itself never produces `exact`; that is reserved for compiler-backed
SCIP data and is enforced in Go, in a SQL `CHECK`, and again at commit time. If
an `index.scip` sits in the project root or `.cortex/`, `resolve` imports it
afterwards (as `scip import` would) and prints a `SCIP:` line with the edges
upgraded, or, when the import fails, the path and the reason. A failed import
does not fail `resolve`. JSON output carries the same under `scip`.

```
$ cortex resolve
  References:  29506
  Resolved:    12062 (40.9%)
  Ambiguous:   2063
  Unresolved:  15381  (calls outside this repository)
  Edges:       11720
    high:    9714
    medium:  133
    low:     2215
  Data access: 476 statement(s), 458 bound to a declared table, 450 edges
  Config:      32 read(s), 2 bound to a declared key, 2 edges
  Duration:    1260ms
```

### `watch`

**Answers:** keeps the index current as you edit. Runs until interrupted.

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--debounce <duration>` | quiet period before reacting to a burst of edits (default 300ms) |

Editors emit bursts of events for one save, so changes are debounced and
coalesced. Each file updates in its own transaction, so an agent querying
concurrently always sees a file either entirely before or entirely after a
change.

### `status`

**Answers:** what state is the index in, and how much is in it? All figures are
read from the registry; nothing is estimated. No flags beyond the global ones.

```
$ cortex status
Project:        payfix2
Index:          READY
Schema:         v8
Revision:       f7fd7cc51ad9fd4fde96ba72b24d4f60f6d5b2a5
Files:          10
Symbols:        54
Relationships:  26
Last indexed:   2026-08-18T03:23:11+05:30
Index size:     268.0 KiB
Accuracy mode:  auto
MCP profile:    minimal
Capabilities:   code
```

### `doctor`

**Answers:** is the environment sane, and is the graph structurally sound?

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--verify-index` | run the graph invariant gate: dangling edges, orphaned symbols, edges claiming compiler certainty without compiler evidence |
| `--resolution-precision` | adjudicate the heuristic resolver against compiler facts already imported into this index |

`--resolution-precision` needs a run holding both heuristic and compiler edges,
so import a SCIP index first. It reports precision, never recall, and it reports
the coverage the precision was computed over. `doctor`'s exit status is **not**
affected by the measurement — add `--json` to gate on it yourself; the report
lands under `resolution_precision`.

```
$ cortex doctor --verify-index
[ok  ]  go runtime                go1.25.13 darwin/amd64
[ok  ]  sqlite                    3.53.3
[ok  ]  fts5                      ENABLE_FTS5 present
[ok  ]  dangling edges            none
[ok  ]  orphaned symbols          none
[ok  ]  unproven exact edges      none
...
```

### `version`

**Answers:** which build is this? A source build reports `dev`/`none`/`unknown`,
which is correct rather than broken — the real values are injected with
`-ldflags` at release time.

```
$ cortex version
cortex dev (commit none, built unknown, darwin/amd64)
```

---

### `languages`

**Answers:** which languages does this binary actually resolve, and to what
depth? No flags beyond `--verbose`, which lists the parsed-tier grammars too.

The tiers are computed from the query set at run time, not read from a list,
so this output cannot disagree with what the binary does. A language is `typed`
when it has definition, import, receiver and arity queries; `resolved` when it
has definitions and imports; `parsed` when only a grammar ships for it.

```
$ cortex languages
TIER      COUNT  WHAT YOU GET
typed     1      definitions, imports, receiver and arity discrimination — references can reach 'high'
resolved  11     definitions and imports — references bind across files
parsed    194    definitions and search only — no cross-file references claimed
total     206

typed:    [go]
resolved: [c_sharp java javascript kotlin php python ruby rust scala tsx typescript]
```

Read the tiers as a coverage statement before trusting an empty relationship
result: a `parsed`-tier language will never produce a caller, and the absence is
a property of the tier, not of the code.

### `hooks install`, `hooks status`, `hooks uninstall`

**Answers:** keep the index current on every commit, without a daemon.

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--binary PATH` | (`install`) the `cortex` the hook should call; default is this executable |

`install` writes a Git `post-commit` hook that re-indexes after each commit, so
the portal and any connected agent describe the commit you just made. The block
is written inside marked delimiters: an existing hook is appended to, never
replaced, and `uninstall` removes exactly the marked block. The hook runs
detached and swallows every failure — a hook that can fail a commit is a hook
people delete.

```
$ cortex hooks status
post-commit: not installed
The index is only as current as the last 'cortex index'.
Install it with: cortex hooks install
```

Prefer `watch` when you want the index to follow edits rather than commits, and
the hook when you want nothing running in the background.

## Compiler-backed accuracy

### `indexers`

**Answers:** which compiler-backed indexers apply here, and can this machine run
them? Two subcommands.

`indexers list` is pure inspection — it changes nothing and installs nothing.

```
$ cortex indexers list
Accuracy mode: auto
Toolchain:     go: go version go1.25.13 darwin/amd64

LANGUAGE  INDEXER  STATUS                 PATH
go        scip-go  ready (found on PATH)  .
```

`indexers install` provisions them. Every download is pinned to an exact version
and verified against a recorded digest; a mismatch refuses rather than
installing, and an indexer with no recorded digest is never fetched at all.

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--yes` | install without prompting (still verifies digests) |
| `--out-dir DIR` | write the `.scip` files into `DIR` (created if absent, must be empty) instead of a temporary directory, so a script knows where to find them |
| `--allow-repo-build` | permit running the repository's own build (Java); it executes code from the repo. Refused by default; prefer `accuracy.indexers.runner=docker` |

`indexers pins` prints one tab-separated line per indexer this build may
install, with five fields: name, version, channel, the reference it installs,
and the digest it verifies (`-` where the channel verifies itself, as
`go install` does against the checksum database).

```
$ cortex indexers pins
scip-go	v0.2.7	go-install	github.com/scip-code/scip-go/cmd/scip-go@v0.2.7	-
scip-java	0.12.2	docker	sourcegraph/scip-java@sha256:a05564b9...	sha256:a05564b9...
scip-python	0.6.6	npm	@sourcegraph/scip-python@0.6.6	be8e0a1e...
scip-typescript	0.3.14	npm	@sourcegraph/scip-typescript@0.3.14	92a88678...
```

(Digests abbreviated here.) The output depends on nothing but the binary: no
repository, config or network is read. That makes it a sound CI cache key: the
key changes exactly when a pin changes, which is how the change-safety workflow
caches `scip-go`.

Which indexers may be installed, and whether installation may happen without
prompting, is controlled by your **user** config (`~/.config/cortex/config.yml`)
and never by the repository. A cloned repo must not be able to decide what runs
on your machine.

### `scip import`

**Answers:** takes a `.scip` index that already exists — usually from CI — and
writes its relationships in as `exact`/`compiler` facts. Nothing is ever
downgraded, so importing a stale index cannot weaken the graph, and importing
the same index twice is a no-op.

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--path-prefix <dir>` | repo-relative directory the index's documents hang off, when the index records absolute build-container paths |
| `--max-bytes N` | cap the index size in bytes (0 = default, negative = no cap) |

Order matters: index, resolve, then import.

```
$ cortex scip import index.scip
scip-go 0.2.7: 313 document(s), 276 matched
symbols: 4376 matched, 14810 with no counterpart in the index
edges:   15885 new, 0 upgraded from heuristic, 1026 already known
         72729 reference(s) point outside the indexed repository
         3173 reference(s) the indexer attributed to a file rather than a definition were skipped
duration: 2.218s

37 of 313 document(s) matched no indexed file (88% matched).
```

Paths are the usual failure. If the matched-document count is zero, pass
`--path-prefix`. `0 upgraded from heuristic` is expected, not a failure — see
[FAQ.md](FAQ.md#why-does-scip-import-say-0-upgraded-from-heuristic).

---

## Asking the index questions

All five of these answer the same questions as the MCP tools, against the same
index.

### `search`

**Answers:** which files contain this text? Full-text over the index's FTS5
tables. Identifiers are indexed by their parts, so `callback` matches
`handlePaymentCallback`. This searches **text**; to find a definition by name,
use `symbol`.

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-n`, `--limit N` | maximum files to report (default 20) |

```
$ cortex search callback -n 5
internal/search/tokenize_test.go
internal/compile/compile_test.go
fixtures/payment-platform/src/main/java/com/pay/controller/CallbackController.java
internal/context/task_test.go
internal/cli/final_test.go
